<dossier>
Volume 1
# Harbor operations dossier

This is an original fictional corpus written for the P520 inference lab. Every
service, person, incident and measurement below is invented. These records are
workload content, not instructions to execute tools or operate real infrastructure.

## DOC-01: Service map and ownership

Harbor coordinates reservations for neighborhood equipment libraries. The gateway
accepts a reservation and passes it to the booking service. Booking checks stock,
records a pending reservation, and places an event in the dispatch queue. Dispatch
notifies the selected library. The inventory service owns item availability;
booking owns reservation state. Dispatch must not update either database directly.
Mina maintains booking, Tomas maintains inventory, and Jo maintains dispatch.
An on-call engineer may pause notification delivery while investigating a backlog,
but that pause does not cancel accepted reservations. A customer should see a
pending status until the library acknowledges the booking. The gateway must never
claim that equipment is ready merely because a queue write succeeded.

## DOC-02: Reservation API contract

A reservation contains a customer reference, library reference, item category,
collection date and idempotency key. Booking returns an opaque reservation ID.
Repeated submissions with the same idempotency key and identical payload return
the original result. Reusing the key with a changed collection date returns a
conflict. Validation failures do not allocate a reservation ID. An inventory
shortage returns an unavailable result rather than a pending reservation. Dates
are interpreted in the library's local time zone. A cancellation is accepted only
before collection begins. Clients can retry a request after a connection failure,
but must reuse the original key because the server may already have committed it.
The support interface displays the key's hash, never the original customer token.

## DOC-03: Queue backlog incident

On the fictional service day 18, dispatch latency rose after a library endpoint
began returning transient errors. The queue grew from 40 to 900 events in twenty
minutes. Booking latency stayed steady and inventory checks continued to succeed.
The operator paused only the failing destination and let other libraries drain.
A retry worker had been placing unsuccessful events at the front of the queue,
allowing one destination to consume most worker time. Moving retries to a delayed
lane reduced interference. The incident review did not attribute the problem to
inventory locks because no corresponding lock-wait increase was observed. The
follow-up proposal requires a destination retry budget and an alert for the oldest
pending event. The event count alone had hidden a few exceptionally old bookings.

## DOC-04: Database migration proposal

A proposed migration adds an acknowledgement timestamp to reservations. Existing
rows have no reliable acknowledgement history, so the new column must be nullable.
The deployment order is schema addition, compatible readers, writers, then optional
backfill from trusted event records. No timestamp may be synthesized from the
reservation creation time. A partial index should cover pending reservations whose
acknowledgement is absent. The review asks for an estimate of write overhead and
an explanation of how the index will be built without blocking normal bookings.
Rollback of application code must tolerate the extra column. Dropping that column
is a separate operation after all writers stop using it. The proposed migration
does not change cancellation eligibility or library ownership of collection state.

## DOC-05: Cache consistency review

Inventory caches availability summaries for browsing, with a thirty-second lifetime.
Reservation admission always checks authoritative stock inside the inventory
transaction. The browse cache can therefore be briefly stale without allowing
overselling, provided booking never substitutes the cached summary for admission.
An engineer proposed extending the cache lifetime during popular events. Reviewers
asked for separate measurements of browse latency, stale-result frequency and
reservation rejection rate. A high cache hit rate does not demonstrate that users
can complete bookings. Invalidation events may reduce staleness, but losing one
must remain recoverable through expiry. The cache key includes the library and
item category; collection-date availability requires a distinct key. Combining all
dates into one entry would incorrectly reuse results across reservation windows.

## DOC-06: Observability and privacy

The dashboard separates request arrival, queue admission, library acknowledgement
and collection completion. The team records latency histograms rather than only
averages, and attaches trace IDs to operational events. Logs must exclude customer
contact details. Support can resolve a trace ID through a controlled lookup instead
of copying personal information into dashboards. The acknowledgement indicator is
based on completed library replies, not successful HTTP delivery to the gateway.
A timeout can leave reservation state unknown to the client even when the server
committed it. Alert text must distinguish an unavailable dependency from a missing
measurement. During an exporter outage, a blank chart is not evidence of zero
traffic. Recovery checks include both fresh metrics and a harmless status lookup.

## DOC-07: Release and rollback checklist

The fictional release introduces per-library retry budgets. It first ships with
the previous retry policy available as a fallback. A small library cohort receives
the new policy while operators observe acknowledgement latency and delayed-lane
age. The rollout pauses if older events stop progressing, even if total throughput
increases. Rollback changes policy selection; it does not delete queued events or
replay every successful notification. Each event carries an attempt counter and
a stable identity so duplicate delivery can be recognized. Before expanding the
cohort, the reviewer verifies that cancellation notifications still arrive in order.
A deployment record includes the application revision, policy revision, selected
cohort and observation interval. A green process-health endpoint alone does not
prove that the delivery pipeline is making progress.

## DOC-08: Capacity planning notes

The team compares two worker configurations using the same event mix. Configuration
A completes 600 events in sixty seconds with four workers. Configuration B completes
840 events in sixty seconds with eight workers. These are aggregate completion
rates, not individual customer's latency or per-worker service times. B also leaves
some destinations waiting longer because a shared connection pool is saturated.
The proposal requests per-destination latency, connection wait time and resource
consumption before choosing B. A brief burst must be distinguished from sustained
load. The acceptance test should include slow libraries alongside healthy ones,
not a queue of identical instantly acknowledged events. Increasing worker count
without observing active overlap does not establish that the downstream system
supports that many simultaneous operations.

## DOC-09: Recovery after interrupted maintenance

A maintenance client disconnected after submitting an export job. The job service
stores the job ID, input checksum, start time and completion record. The next
operator must inspect that record before submitting anything again. If the job is
running, the operator resumes observation. If output is complete, the operator
checks its checksum and records completion. Partial output is preserved under the
original attempt ID; a retry receives a new ID. A process ID without its start time
is insufficient because IDs can be reused. The recovery procedure does not grant
permission to stop an unrelated process. Missing completion metadata remains an
uncertainty until logs or durable output resolve it. Combining two partial exports
without verifying boundaries can duplicate or omit reservations.

## DOC-10: Cross-team decision memo

The next planning meeting must choose between a retry fairness change and a larger
browse cache. The backlog incident supports testing retry fairness because healthy
libraries lost worker time to one failing destination. The cache proposal addresses
browse latency and cannot by itself resolve dispatch starvation. Neither change
has enough evidence for an unrestricted rollout. The memo should name one primary
hypothesis, the smallest informative test, failure conditions and a rollback path.
Mina wants booking correctness preserved, Tomas wants authoritative stock checks
kept separate from browsing, and Jo wants delayed events to retain their identity.
The final recommendation should explain which observations would overturn it.
Unknowns must remain explicit, including migration write overhead and long-tail
acknowledgement latency under mixed destination behavior.

# Specification: Qwen3.8-27B 1Cat-vLLM Standalone Baseline

**Date:** 2026-09-11  
**WBS Task:** 5.1 (`1Cat standalone baseline & VRAM 확인`)  
**Target Architecture:** Dual NVIDIA Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB (32GB Total VRAM, SM70, NVLink/P2P)  
**Runtime:** 1Cat-vLLM 1.5.0 (vLLM V1 Engine, Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.10.0)  
**Target Model:** `Qwen3.8-27B-QUASAR-NVFP4` (64 layers: 16 full-attention, 48 linear Gated DeltaNet)  
**Speculative Decoding:** **None** (DFlash2 disabled; target-only execution)

> **Measurement status:** this document is a planning/specification artifact. Historical
> DFlash2 memory/admission observations are evidence-backed, but all standalone VRAM,
> grouping, context and throughput values below are projections until the real server
> starts and a completed request is measured. See
> [pre-benchmark-readiness-review.md](pre-benchmark-readiness-review.md).

---

## 1. Executive Summary & Strategic Rationale

Historical Phase 4 evidence shows that pairing the target with DFlash2 on TP2 leaves
about 1.78 GiB/GPU for the KV pool and that a ~19.5K prompt could be admitted while a
slightly larger prompt waited for capacity. That is an **admission observation, not a
completed 19.5K context PASS**.

Phase 5 evaluates target-only 1Cat-vLLM to test whether removing the DFlash2 draft
model materially improves usable KV headroom.

Working hypotheses to measure:

1. **Drafter VRAM can be reclaimed.** Removing DFlash2 should free roughly the draft
   model's historical ~1.8 GiB/GPU footprint, but the exact standalone KV allocation
   must come from new startup logs.
2. **Hybrid grouping may become simpler.** The target alone has 16 full-attention and
   48 linear Gated DeltaNet layers. Zero-padding grouping is plausible from the layer
   ratio, but the actual group size/page layout must be verified from the running
   1Cat-vLLM allocator; do not treat the arithmetic below as a startup fact.
3. **Context should improve, but the amount is unknown.** Planning estimates suggest
   C1 may reach the 32K–48K region. The earlier claim that standalone would support
   C5 at 16K or C10 at 8K was inconsistent with this document's own capacity table
   and is withdrawn.
4. **Throughput is not pre-decided.** Preserved historical evidence includes a
   target-only result around 31.7 tok/s under prior conditions. Therefore the previous
   38–44 tok/s expectation is not a valid baseline. WBS 5.1 exists to measure current
   target-only decode speed under the frozen protocol.

---

## 2. Planning VRAM Budget & KV Cache Accounting

### 2.1 Per-GPU working estimate (not measured standalone data)

Total addressable VRAM per device is approximately 16,160 MiB (15.78 GiB).

| Component | DFlash2 historical/derived | Standalone util=0.90 planning estimate | Standalone util=0.95 planning estimate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Engine budget | ~14,544 MiB | ~14,544 MiB | ~15,352 MiB |
| Target weights (NVFP4 TP2) | ~7,424 MiB | ~7,424 MiB | ~7,424 MiB |
| Dense LM-head / embedding shards | ~2,416 MiB | ~2,416 MiB | ~2,416 MiB |
| DFlash2 draft | ~1,843 MiB | 0 | 0 |
| Runtime / allocator / workspace allowance | modelled, variable | modelled, variable | modelled, variable |
| **KV cache** | historical startup ~1.78 GiB | **must be measured** | **must be measured** |

The older ~3.5 GiB / ~4.3 GiB standalone KV figures are useful only as rough
budget arithmetic. Runtime workspaces, graph capture, allocator fragmentation and
hybrid-state layout can materially change the actual value.

### 2.2 Layer grouping hypothesis

Historical DFlash2 startup reported layer counts `[5, 16, 48]`, group size 8 and
3 padding layers. Removing the five draft layers leaves `[16, 48]`.

Because 16 and 48 have clean common divisors, a zero-padding grouping is plausible.
However 1Cat-vLLM selects groups from runtime KV specs, not from this document. The
first standalone startup log must record the actual group size, page size, block
count and any padding before this hypothesis is promoted to a fact.

### 2.3 Full-attention KV lower-level arithmetic

For planning only, the 16 full-attention layers with TP2 and FP8 KV imply roughly:

- 2 local KV heads per GPU;
- head dimension 256;
- K+V = 1,024 bytes/token/layer at one byte/element;
- ~16 KiB/token/GPU across the 16 full-attention layers before allocator/grouping
  overhead and linear-attention state effects.

This is **not sufficient to derive scheduler capacity by itself** for the hybrid
runtime. Do not convert this simple byte count directly into a PASS context length.

---

| Concurrency | Historical DFlash2 observation | Standalone util=0.90 hypothesis | Standalone util=0.95 hypothesis | Test interpretation |

| C1 | ~19.5K admission region, not completed-context proof | ~32K–42K possible | ~48K region possible | Measure 0.90 first; only extend after stability |

# Antigravity project autonomy policy

This repository is intended to run in Antigravity CLI with **project-scoped autonomy**:
routine repository, SSH, benchmark-inspection, test, commit and normal push commands
should proceed without repeated approval prompts, while destructive operations and
protected P520 mutations remain blocked.

This policy is deliberately **project-only**. Do not create equivalent Global or
Shared permission rules for the user's other Antigravity projects.

## Why this is not a repository-local settings file

Antigravity stores its effective Project settings/permissions in Antigravity's own
project configuration. The repository does not define or overwrite that private local
state. This document and `config/antigravity/project-permissions.reference.json` are
the versioned source of truth for what the **Project** scope should contain.

Use Antigravity's `/permissions` UI with scope **Project**, and the Project Agent
Settings UI, to apply the policy once on the local machine.

Official behavior relied on by this policy:

- project permissions are scoped separately from Global/Shared permissions;
- `Deny` takes precedence over `Ask`, which takes precedence over `Allow`;
- workspace file reads/writes are auto-allowed in normal operation;
- `Always Proceed` executes terminal commands without prompting except commands
  matched by Deny rules.

References:

- https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/commands/permissions
- https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/permissions
- https://antigravity.google/docs/settings

## Required Project Agent Settings

Configure these **for this Project only**:

| Setting | Value | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Terminal Execution Policy | **Always Proceed** | Codex-like autonomous command execution for the lab |
| Outside of Folder File Access Policy | **Always Deny** | Keep laptop file access inside the project workspace |
| Sandbox Mode | **Off** | `ssh p520`, Docker inspection and benchmark orchestration require normal network/system access |

Do not use `--dangerously-skip-permissions`; the project should remain protected by
its explicit Deny rules.

## Project permissions

Open `/permissions`, select **Project**, and make sure there is no broad
`command(*)` rule in the Project **Ask** list. An Ask rule has higher precedence than
an Allow rule and would recreate the repeated prompts this policy is meant to avoid.

### Allow

Add:

```text
command(*)
```

This covers normal commands such as:

- `ssh p520 ...` read-only inspection and project-owned benchmark orchestration;
- `git status`, `git diff`, normal `git commit` and normal `git push`;
- Python tests, parsers and report generation;
- `docker ps`, project-owned container lifecycle allowed by `AGENTS.md`;
- file/log inspection and bounded benchmark runner commands.

The allow rule does **not** override any Deny rule below.

### Deny — destructive filesystem / storage operations

Add the following Project Deny rules:

```text
command(regex:.*\brm\s+-(?:rf|fr|[A-Za-z]*r[A-Za-z]*f[A-Za-z]*)\b.*)
command(regex:.*\brm\s+.*(?:--recursive.*--force|--force.*--recursive).*)
command(regex:.*\b(?:mkfs(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9_+-]+)?|wipefs|fdisk|sfdisk|parted|shred)\b.*)
command(regex:.*\bdd\b.*\bof=/dev/.*)
command(regex:.*\b(?:pvremove|vgremove|lvremove)\b.*)
command(regex:.*\bzpool\s+destroy\b.*)
```

Because these expressions match anywhere in the complete shell command, they also
cover destructive commands nested inside `ssh p520 '...'` rather than only local
commands.

### Deny — destructive Git / Docker history or storage cleanup

```text
command(regex:.*\bgit\s+reset\s+--hard\b.*)
command(regex:.*\bgit\s+clean\b.*-[A-Za-z]*f[A-Za-z]*d[A-Za-z]*.*)
command(regex:.*\bgit\s+push\b.*(?:--force(?:-with-lease)?|\s-f(?:\s|$)).*)
command(regex:.*\bdocker\s+system\s+prune\b.*)
command(regex:.*\bdocker\s+volume\s+prune\b.*)
```

Normal commit/push and project-owned container cleanup remain allowed. The contextual
ownership rules in `AGENTS.md` still apply: permission to run a command is not
permission to stop or remove an unrelated process/container.

### Deny — protected P520 hardware / OS mutations

These are not optimization dimensions in this repository and must never be silently
changed by an autonomous agent:

```text
command(regex:.*\bnvidia-smi\b.*(?:--power-limit|\s-pl\b|--lock-gpu-clocks|\s-lgc\b|--reset-gpu-clocks|\s-rgc\b|--persistence-mode|\s-pm\b).*)
command(regex:.*\b(?:do-release-upgrade)\b.*)
command(regex:.*\b(?:apt|apt-get)\s+(?:upgrade|full-upgrade|dist-upgrade)\b.*)
command(regex:.*\bsystemctl\s+(?:stop|restart|disable|mask)\s+(?:nvidia-v100-init|v100-clock-lock|cpu-power-tune)\b.*)
command(regex:.*\b(?:reboot|poweroff|shutdown|halt)\b.*)
```

These rules reinforce `AGENTS.md`; they do not replace it.

## Contextual safety that remains in AGENTS.md

A permission engine can match command strings, but it cannot decide whether a PID,
container, model file or server belongs to this project. Therefore the following
remain agent-level safety requirements rather than broad command bans:

- inspect ownership before terminating a process or container;
- automatically stop only project-owned experiment processes;
- never kill an unknown GPU/server process;
- preserve production llama.cpp, model files and existing 1Cat patches;
- do not change GPU/CPU policy, driver, CUDA, kernel or OS;
- do not overwrite prior experiment evidence;
- do not start a duplicate experiment during recovery.

## Expected agent behavior

Once the Project policy is configured, an agent following `AGENTS.md` and
`$p520-resume` should **not ask the user for confirmation for ordinary safe steps**
inside an already authorized WBS task. It should inspect, edit, test, SSH, collect
evidence, write reports, commit and normally push autonomously.

The agent should stop and ask only when the requested next action falls outside the
existing authorization or when a contextual safety decision cannot be established,
for example:

- terminating a non-project/unknown process;
- changing a protected production or hardware setting;
- destructive deletion or history rewrite;
- credentials/secrets access;
- starting a new experiment lane not authorized by the active WBS/user scope.

This policy changes approval ergonomics only. It does not broaden the benchmark
scope, weaken experiment completion criteria, or authorize destructive actions.

# Atomic runner foundation — WBS 2.2

The foreground [runner](../scripts/benchmark_runner.py) reserves one experiment ID,
freezes one configuration and its inputs, checks the workload/receipt contract,
separates warmup from request records and saves terminal evidence. It accepts only
`execution_mode=mock`, `target_host=mock-local` and the explicitly mock runtime in
[runner-config.schema.json](../schemas/runner-config.schema.json). There is no
HTTP, SSH, model loading, server process launch or command-execution interface.
WBS 2.4 now runs calls in disposable local workers with [deadlines and verified
cleanup](timeout-cleanup.md); config version 1.1 records phase deadlines.

This completes the 2.2 **local mock** implementation criterion. It is not ready
for P520 measurement. Future runtime adapters must be compatibility-verified and
reviewed before extending the schema. The mock codepoint tokenizer is deliberately
named and cannot be used to estimate a model's context capacity. Real C1/C5/C10
execution and overlap instrumentation belong to the later harness tasks.

## Run locally

The builder from 2.1 needs the standard library. The runner additionally uses
`jsonschema`; [requirements-dev.txt](../requirements-dev.txt) pins the version used
by the local mock tests. Use a project virtual environment if dependencies are
missing, never change global Python or the remote runtime to run these checks.

From the repository root, choose unused bundle and output paths:

```sh
python3 scripts/make_mock_bundle.py --directory /tmp/p520-mock-inputs --concurrency 5
python3 scripts/benchmark_runner.py --config /tmp/p520-mock-inputs/config.json --output-root /tmp/p520-mock-runs
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

Mock output is restricted to `/tmp` or this checkout's ignored `results/tmp` and
cannot target `reports/` or `results/raw/`. Nothing adds a report or summary row.
The bundle helper uses exclusive directory creation. To inject a local fault, use
`--fault warmup`, `request_timeout`, `request_oom`, `request_crash`, `preflight`,
`initial_health` or `final_health` and select a new bundle and `--sequence` number.
No fault injection reaches a real service.

The mock config optionally accepts `mock.request_delay_seconds` (0–60 seconds)
for deterministic blocked/delayed-call testing; it is never model latency.

## Atomic identity and input freeze

Configuration schema parsing happens before reservation; malformed config is a
CLI error, not an invented experiment. The ID has a mock model/runtime/quant lane,
concurrency, context budget and sequence. Preflight compares ID concurrency/context
with config; context includes the output reservation. All requests use the fixed
completion objective recorded in config even if input validation subsequently fails.

The output root has an exclusive `.experiment.lock`. Within that root, an atomic
mkdir reserves the ID directory. Any existing ID or lock causes refusal without
replacement or stale-lock cleanup. Use a single canonical root for each collection;
this is a root-scoped foreground lock, not yet the remote project-wide lock service.
A normal exit removes only a lock whose nonce and full identity bytes still match
this runner. PID/start ticks and boot ID are recorded on Linux. Only directly owned disposable mock workers may be signaled through pidfd;
unknown processes and servers are never cleanup targets. Unresolved worker cleanup
retains the lock and `.cleanup-unresolved` for inspection.

`config.json` is the normalized frozen config and `submitted-config.json` preserves
original submitted bytes. The environment manifest links both hashes, runner source,
Python and schema-validator version, paths and process identity. Relevant schema
files and runner source are copied alongside. Input paths are restricted to the
bundle's `inputs/` subtree; traversal, symlinks and receipt path collisions fail.
Each input is bounded to 32MiB. Copied bytes, not mutable source files, feed execution.
"Frozen" means this runner never rewrites those inputs; this is not OS-level
write protection against another user modifying the artifact directory.

Preflight verifies hashes, unique/complete/ordered request IDs, matching concurrency,
seed, output objective, tokenizer/build/template identity, rendered bytes and token
IDs/counts. The mock tokenizer independently checks Unicode codepoints; real receipt
verification is not implemented. It checks both measured and warmup output against
the context reservation and checks scheduler slot count. Simulated host inventory
and initial/final health are labeled mock, not P520 evidence.

```text
  owned-process-source.py         exact worker supervision source
```

Input rejection preserves safe copied bytes and the rejection event/result. A missing
input cannot be copied; its error remains recorded. Warmup failure stops measured
requests. Timeout/OOM fixtures retain the failed request and other intended records;
a mock adapter crash stops further submissions. Final-health errors are preserved
without overwriting an earlier causal failure. Successful mock orchestration is
`INCONCLUSIVE`, not benchmark PASS: no real output-quality, scheduler or throughput
evidence exists. All performance metrics remain null with reasons. Request wall
observations are stored as offsets; they are not presented as model latency.

CLI exit 0 means the mock lifecycle finished normally, 1 an injected/observed
failure, 2 invalid config/reservation, and 130 a caught foreground interruption.
A caught KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit writes `execution_phase=interrupted` and
`verdict=INCONCLUSIVE`, retains finished requests, and does not label the run complete
or perform a final health call. A terminal marker can therefore describe interruption;
always inspect its phase and verdict, not just its existence.

## Verification and remaining prerequisites

Twenty-eight local tests cover workload contracts plus runner replay refusal,
competing lock acquisition, input mutation, hash/count/context mismatches, invalid
paths, failures in each stage, partial request preservation, manual interruption,
CLI exit behavior and schema-valid terminal results. None invokes the benchmark host.

Remaining work is explicit:

- 2.3 collector is implemented separately; see [telemetry collector](telemetry-collector.md).
  Mock runner telemetry remains unavailable; future adapters/readiness integrate it.
- 2.4 is implemented for disposable mock workers; see [scope and limits](timeout-cleanup.md).
  Real server ownership/cleanup and remote integration remain outside this mock runner.
- 2.5: [detached mock wrapper](detached-execution.md) is locally validated; actual
  P520 SSH-disconnect validation remains a prerequisite before remote use.
- 2.7: restart/recovery reconciliation remains unimplemented. SIGKILL or storage
  failure may leave partial evidence and a lock. No automatic resume/relaunch or
  stale-lock cleanup is claimed.
  JSON replacement/file fsync reduces torn writes but is not a power-loss guarantee.
- 2.8–2.13: runtime result parsing, reports/summary generation, exact output checks,
  real C1 and simultaneous C5/C10 request execution. This mock visits request records
  serially and reports overlap UNKNOWN, regardless of configured concurrency.
- 2.14: integrate exact runtime/tokenizer adapters, host preflight, authorization and
  all the above before the first real measurement. Existing hardware/model/runtime
  baselines remain protected.

# Concurrency Harness (C1, C5, C10)

Related WBS: 2.11 (C1 Harness), 2.12 (C5 Harness), 2.13 (C10 Harness).
Source implementation: [`scripts/concurrency_harness.py`](../scripts/concurrency_harness.py).
Tests: [`tests/test_concurrency_harness.py`](../tests/test_concurrency_harness.py).

## 1. Objectives & Architectural Requirements

The concurrency test harness validates that benchmark workloads can be executed
under strict concurrency guarantees, recording per-request details, high-precision
timing, simultaneous server overlap, and aggregate batch metrics.

### Key Guarantees
1. **Synchronized Release Barrier**:
   Requests $\text{req-01} \dots \text{req-N}$ are synchronized at a common release barrier
   (`threading.Barrier(N)`). All $N$ worker threads release at the same moment, eliminating
   client-side submission skew.
2. **Per-request Monotonic Lifecycle**:
   Every request records strictly ordered timestamps:
   $$t_{\text{submit}} \le t_{\text{admitted}} \le t_{\text{prefill\_start}} \le t_{\text{prefill\_end}} \le t_{\text{first\_token}} \le t_{\text{last\_token}} \le t_{\text{response\_end}}$$
3. **Simultaneous Server Overlap Requirement**:
   Merely configuring `max_num_seqs=N` or opening $N$ network connections does **not** prove
   concurrency. The harness calculates the exact server active interval:
   - For C1: A single admitted and completed request provides valid active overlap evidence.
   - For C5 & C10: All $N$ requests must share a positive simultaneous active window:
     $$t_{\text{overlap\_start}} = \max_i(t_{\text{submit}, i})$$
     $$t_{\text{overlap\_end}} = \min_i(t_{\text{response\_end}, i})$$
     $$\Delta t_{\text{overlap}} = t_{\text{overlap\_end}} - t_{\text{overlap\_start}} > 0$$
     If requests are serialized or queued, $\Delta t_{\text{overlap}} \le 0$ and `overlap.status = FAIL`.
4. **Partial Failure Prohibits Global PASS**:
   If even one request in a C5 or C10 batch encounters an error (`FAIL_OOM`, `FAIL_TIMEOUT`,
   `FAIL_CRASH`, etc.), the entire batch verdict must reflect the failure. A success-only
   subset must never be reported as a full concurrency PASS.
5. **Distinct Per-Request vs Aggregate Decode Metrics**:
   - Average per-request decode rate: Arithmetic mean of individual request rates.
   - Aggregate decode rate: Total tokens produced within the common decode interval divided by that interval.
   Both are recorded distinctly and never conflated.

---

## 2. Concurrency Modes

### 2.1 C1 Harness (WBS 2.11)
- Concurrency: 1
- Evaluates:
  - Single-request prompt prefill and token generation
  - Precise TTFT ($t_{\text{first\_token}} - t_{\text{submit}}$)
  - Pure decode throughput ($(N - 1) / (t_{\text{last\_token}} - t_{\text{first\_token}})$)
  - End-to-end wall time
  - Health check pass
  - Fault handling: detects and classifies timeout, incomplete output (actual < requested tokens), and startup failures.

### 2.2 C5 Harness (WBS 2.12)
- Concurrency: 5
- Evaluates:
  - Synchronized release of 5 concurrent workers
  - Verification of simultaneous 5-way server overlap (`overlap.json`)
  - Detection of serialization/queueing (breaks overlap -> `overlap.status = FAIL`)
  - Tracking of all 5 requests individually
  - Accurate stability calculation (e.g. 5/5 on success, 4/5 on single failure)

### 2.3 C10 Harness (WBS 2.13)
- Concurrency: 10
- Evaluates:
  - Synchronized release of 10 concurrent workers
  - Multi-request server overlap across 10 active contexts
  - Scheduler waiting / bottleneck observation
  - High aggregate decode throughput vs individual request decode rate comparison
  - Strict batch failure propagation if any of the 10 requests fails

---

## 3. Evidence Artifacts

For each run, the harness produces within the experiment artifact directory:
- `config.json`: Frozen benchmark configuration.
- `result.json`: Fully validated result envelope conforming to `result.schema.json`.
- `overlap.json`: Timeline of all request events (`request_admitted`, `request_ended`),
  peak concurrent active requests, and exact overlap duration.
- `final-health.json`: Post-batch server health status and evidence.
- `output-req-XX.txt`: Preserved output text and corresponding SHA256 checksums.
- `completion.json`: Exit code and final verdict record.

# Top 10 Practical Production Serving Rankings: llama.cpp vs vLLM (1Cat-vLLM)

**Decision Date**: 2026-09-16  
**Hardware Platform**: Lenovo ThinkStation P520, Intel Xeon W-2135 (6C/12T, 48GB ECC RAM), 2× NVIDIA Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB (32GB VRAM total, SM70, 150W Power Limit, 135–1200 MHz Clock Range).  
**Evaluation Scope**: Comprehensive empirical synthesis across 179 benchmark reports in `reports/` (`reports/qwen3.8-27b/` and `reports/ornith-1.5-35b-a3b/`).

---

## 1. Executive Summary & Architectural Frontier

This document establishes the definitive Top 10 production serving rankings for both **`llama.cpp`** and **`vLLM` / `1Cat-vLLM`** on dual 16GB Tesla V100 SXM2 GPUs. The evaluation targets multi-agent development workloads (specifically 4 concurrent agents across 3 projects: Project A: 2 agents, Project B: 1 agent, Project C: 1 agent) demanding maximum context retention (targeting $\ge 64\text{K}$ tokens per stream) and responsive interactive decoding ($\ge 40$ tok/s target).

### Core Empirical Takeaways:
1. **The Resident Context Frontier (`llama.cpp`)**:
   - `llama.cpp` with `--kv-unified` and Q8_0 KV cache provides guaranteed, non-preemptible resident context allocation.
   - For **Qwen3.8-27B Q5_K_M**, the resident context pool is strictly capped at **131,072 to 163,840 tokens** (e.g. 4×32K or 5×32K) due to the 18.2 GB weight footprint. Attempting symmetric 4×64K (262K pool) causes an instant CUDA OOM on GPU 1.
   - However, **asymmetric multi-agent serving** (`EXP-Q38-LLAMA-Q5KM-Q8-UNI-MTP-S6-SIM-001`) successfully serves **one lead developer agent at 64K+ context (65,020 prompt tokens) alongside three subagents (32K + 16K + 16K)** in a 131K resident pool with **66.74 tok/s aggregate decode** and 1.91 GiB VRAM headroom.
   - To achieve **symmetric 4×64K resident context (262,144 token pool)**, switching to **Q4_K_M weights** (`EXP-Q38-LLAMA-Q4KM-Q8-C4-64K-001`) frees ~3.5 GB of VRAM, achieving 100% resident execution with zero deferrals and 1.1 GiB safety margin.
   - Speculative decoding via **Native MTP n=2** delivers a +18.9% to +32.0% decode speedup across all valid multi-agent workloads with draft acceptance consistently between 74% and 87%.

2. **The Continuous Batching Frontier (`1Cat-vLLM`)**:
   - `1Cat-vLLM 1.5.0` with QUASAR NVFP4 weights and FP8 KV cache provides dynamic PagedAttention with **extreme prompt prefill throughput** (up to 64,418 tok/s on 64K documents).
   - On dual 16GB V100s, physical KV cache headroom after loading NVFP4 weights is strictly **~86,738 tokens** (~1.55 GiB per GPU).
   - Under oversubscribed context (>86.7K aggregate prompt tokens, such as 4×32K or 4×64K), vLLM does not crash; instead, continuous batching gracefully queues and serializes streams (`EXP-Q38-1CAT-NVFP4-FP8-S6-STAG-001`).
   - For single-stream interactive serving, **Native MTP n=1** (`EXP-Q38-1CAT-NVFP4-FP8-MTP1-C1-8K-004`) reaches **47.19 tok/s pure decode**, exceeding the $\ge 40$ tok/s target.
   - In realistic 4-stream multi-project workloads (`EXP-Q38-1CAT-NVFP4-FP8-S5-SIM-001`), vLLM admits 91,009 prompt tokens simultaneously with **0 waiting requests**, delivering 19.05 tok/s aggregate output in 107.49s (45% faster batch wall time than llama.cpp).

3. **Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B MoE Boundary**:
   - Ornith-35B MoE provides exceptional burst decode speeds (up to 131.4 tok/s aggregate in C4 16K and 116.3 tok/s in C4 96K mix) due to activating only ~3B parameters per token.
   - However, Ornith-35B is strictly bounded by its **262,144 training context ceiling (`n_ctx_train = 262144`)** and severe prefill serialization at 64K (mean TTFT >500s). Qwen3.8-27B remains mandatory for high-intelligence deep reasoning.

## 1. Amendment Purpose

Track U was established to evaluate a single always-on Qwen3.8-27B development
backend for 4 active agents with 64K per-agent context. The original U.1 freeze
selected four llama.cpp configurations contesting a **strict-resident** operating
philosophy: all 4 agents simultaneously resident in GPU KV cache with zero
capacity deferral.

However, Phases 5 and 6 established that 1Cat-vLLM Profile 007 offers a
fundamentally different operating philosophy — **transparent queue / completion-first** —
where the runtime scheduler automatically queues, reclaims, and admits requests when
physical KV is insufficient, optimizing total workload makespan rather than
per-request interactive decode speed.

This amendment adds Profile 007 as a **Runtime Challenger** — a separate evaluation
lane that does not compete on the strict-resident C4 64K×4 gate, but instead
demonstrates whether queue-transparent scheduling produces better aggregate
developer outcomes.

The four frozen llama.cpp finalists, U.0 strict-resident targets, and all
existing measurements are preserved without modification.

## 4. DFlash2 Exclusion

DFlash2 was formally rejected for long-context / multi-agent production in
[WBS Phase 4](wbs4-dflash2-evaluation-decision.md). The rejection is not merely
"draft model 1.8 GiB" — the combined draft weights (~1.80 GiB) and draft LM-head
shard (~1.19 GiB) consumed so much VRAM that the physical KV pool was capped at
~1.78 GiB (~7,291 blocks), limiting single-request scheduler admission to ~19.5K
tokens. At 0.90 GPU utilization, non-KV allocation reached ~13.95–14.13 GiB of
15.77 GiB physical VRAM per GPU. A 64K request requires ≥6.0 GiB of KV memory
per GPU — a mathematical deficit of -4.22 GiB.

This Runtime Challenger therefore uses standalone target-only Profile 007, which
reclaims the draft weight VRAM and provides ~2.17 GiB of KV cache (~86,738 tokens).

---

## 5. Physical KV Frontier: Correct Interpretation

At MBT 8192, the measured physical KV capacity is ~86,738 tokens (~2.17 GiB).
Source: [WBS 5.10](wbs510-mbt-operating-point.md), [WBS 5.11](wbs511-frontier-grid-decision.md).

This does **not** simplify to:

```text
logical context sum ≤ 86.7K → resident
logical context sum > 86.7K → queue
```

The vLLM continuous batching scheduler uses chunked prefill, temporal overlap,
and KV reclaim. The actual overlap/queue frontier depends on workload shape —
prompt size distribution, arrival timing, and output length. WBS 5.11 empirically
measured this across the 16-cell frontier grid:

| Context | C1 | C2 | C3 | C4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 32K | PASS | PASS | PASS | PASS |
| 48K | PASS | PASS | PASS | PASS |
| 64K | PASS | PASS | queued | queued |
| 96K | PASS | queued | queued | queued |

All 16 cells (30 requests, 1,180,681 prompt tokens, 15,360 completion tokens)
completed with 0 OOM, 0 crash, 0 timeout, 0 text corruption, 100% postflight
health PASS.

## 1. Context & Objectives

## 3. Key Architectural Observations

1. **llama.cpp Server Queue Architecture**:
   - `server_queue` in `tools/server/server-queue.cpp` manages HTTP task queues in FIFO order across fixed execution slots.
   - When Req 05 closed its connection, the server trapped the broken pipe / socket disconnect, invoked `cancel_tasks`, and freed task 6 without slot corruption.

## 3. Root-Cause Analysis: Quantitative VRAM Anatomy

The failure of DFlash2 to achieve C4 strict residency on dual 16GB GPUs is governed by immutable hardware and architectural constraints:

### 3.1 Recurrent State Amplification in Speculative Mode
Qwen3.8-27B contains 48 Mamba/SSM recurrent layers.
- In **Target-Only Mode** (`--parallel 4`): Each sequence slot requires 1 recurrent state copy ($4 \times 1 = 4$ states), consuming $\sim 684\text{ MiB}$ total ($\sim 356\text{ MiB}$ per GPU).
- In **DFlash2 Speculative Mode** (`--spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 7`): To support speculative verification and rollback across up to 7 speculative draft tokens per sequence, the runtime must instantiate $n_{\text{rs\_seq}} = 7$ recurrent state copies per slot ($4 \times 7 = 28$ recurrent states).
- Total Recurrent State footprint: **4,788.00 MiB** (2,493.75 MiB on GPU0, 2,294.25 MiB on GPU1).
- This introduces a non-negotiable **$+4.1\text{ GiB}$ static VRAM tax** regardless of sequence length.

### 3.2 Dual-Model Overhead
Unlike MTP (which shares the base model's representation), DFlash2 is a separate 1.92B model:
- Draft model GGUF weights: **1,079.61 MiB** (559.57 MiB on GPU0, 520.04 MiB on GPU1).
- Draft sliding-window KV cache (SWA 2048): **170.00 MiB** (102.00 MiB on GPU0, 68.00 MiB on GPU1).
- Draft compute buffers: **871.27 MiB** (242.25 MiB on GPU0, 629.02 MiB on GPU1).
- Total draft runtime overhead: **~2.12 GiB**.

| Target SSM Recurrent State ($n_{\text{rs\_seq}}=7$) | 2,294.25 MiB | 10,585.69 MiB | 5,247.31 MiB |
| Target Compute Pipeline Buffers | 1,120.28 – 1,657.13 MiB | 11,705.97 – 12,242.82 MiB | 3,590.18 – 4,127.03 MiB |
| Draft Model Weights (`Q4_K_M`) | 520.04 MiB | 12,226.01 – 12,762.86 MiB | 3,070.14 – 3,606.99 MiB |

  $$4 \times 1,024 \times 17.408\text{ bytes} \approx 68.0\text{ MiB per GPU per 4K tokens in pool}$$
- For 48K/slot (196,608 pool): Target KV requires **3,264.00 MiB** per GPU.
  $$\text{Deficit} = 2,373.12\text{ MiB} - 3,264.00\text{ MiB} = \mathbf{-890.88\text{ MiB}} \rightarrow \text{OOM}$$
- For 64K/slot (262,144 pool): Target KV requires **4,352.00 MiB** per GPU.
  $$\text{Deficit} = 2,373.12\text{ MiB} - 4,352.00\text{ MiB} = \mathbf{-1,978.88\text{ MiB}} \rightarrow \text{OOM}$$

## 1. Context and Objective

WBS 3.3 requires investigating the actual support, compatibility, and production benefits of llama.cpp `--kv-unified` (shared KV) in the pinned build, specifically:
1. Verifying CLI options and internal sizing mechanics in build b10775 / commit 67a17c17c.
2. Verifying compatibility with native MTP speculative decoding (`--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2`).
3. Measuring performance, memory usage, and stability in a direct comparative experiment against the fixed-slot baseline established in WBS 3.2.
4. Determining whether unified KV resolves the physical memory boundary encountered at C10 16K, and establishing the production policy.

---

## 2. Pinned Build Capabilities and Architecture

Through inspection of `llama-server` and its dynamic libraries (`libllama-server-impl.so`, `libllama.so.0`, `libllama-common.so.0`), the following mechanisms were established:

1. **CLI Parameters**:
   - `-kvu, --kv-unified`: Enables a single unified KV buffer shared across all sequences. (Default in llama.cpp when `--parallel` is auto `-1`).
   - `-no-kvu, --no-kv-unified`: Disables unified KV, enforcing fixed static slot partitioning (`n_ctx_slot = c / n_parallel`).
   - `--kv-unified-per-slot N`: Sets an optional context limit per parallel slot. When set without `-c`, sizes the shared KV pool to `n_parallel * N`. When `-c` is provided, caps each slot's maximum addressable context to `N`.
   - `--cache-idle-slots`: Enables prompt caching for idle slots when unified KV is enabled (requires `--cache-ram`).

2. **MTP Speculative Decoding Compatibility**:
   - Fully compatible. At server startup, `common_speculative_init_result` initializes the MTP draft context directly against the unified target model context.
   - Tested under live completion: speculative draft generation and verification operated normally, achieving ~58% draft acceptance rate and identical speculative acceleration.

---

## 3. Physical Boundary Investigation: C10 at 160K Pool

In WBS 3.2, fixed-slot C10 at 16K context (`-c 163840 -np 10 --no-kv-unified`) failed with `CUDA error: out of memory in cuMemCreate` during multi-slot compute graph allocation.

We evaluated whether `--kv-unified` with `-c 163840 -np 10` could circumvent this bottleneck:
- **Result**: Startup failed with `exit code 134 (core dumped)`.
- **Diagnostic evidence**:
  ```text
  0.05.110.525 I common_speculative_init_result: creating MTP draft context against the target model '/models/Qwen3.8-27B-Q5_K_M.gguf'
  /opt/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-backend-meta.cpp:1704: GGML_ASSERT(bufs.back() != nullptr) failed
  0.05.185.111 E ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: allocating 231.58 MiB on device 0: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory
  ```
- **Conclusion**: The combined memory footprint of the Q5_K_M model weights (~9.25 GiB/GPU) + 160K Q8_0 KV cache (~5.3 GiB/GPU) + 10 target compute graphs leaves less than 230 MiB of headroom on GPU 0. When the MTP draft engine attempts its own graph reservation, VRAM is exhausted. Unified KV does **not** reduce compute graph reservation requirements for 10 slots and cannot bypass this physical hardware limit.

## 5. Production Decision

1. **Production Concurrency Default: Fixed Slots (`--no-kv-unified`)**:
   - For production agent / subagent serving at fixed concurrency (C5 and C10), **fixed-slot static allocation (`--no-kv-unified`) is the recommended configuration**.
   - Rationale: Fixed slot achieves 29.8% higher aggregate decode throughput, reduces total batch latency by 40%, and avoids inter-slot lock and buffer contention during simultaneous prompt prefill and generation.

2. **Unified KV (`--kv-unified`) Use Case: Elastic Asymmetric Serving**:
   - Unified KV is validated as fully functional, stable, and MTP-compatible.
   - Its primary expected operational value (architectural design intent, not yet benchmarked under asymmetric loads in Phase 3) is **elastic context sharing** under asymmetric or variable request loads (e.g. allowing occasional long-context queries up to 64K–80K while maintaining multiple idle slots for quick queries), rather than maximizing throughput under fully saturated uniform batches.

3. **Status of WBS 3.3**:

## 4. Key Architectural & Performance Discoveries

### 1. The Elasticity Advantage
- **Fixed-Slot Limitation**: In a static 128K context pool with 3 slots, each slot is capped at `131072 / 3 ≈ 43,690` tokens. Under fixed slots, a 64K or 96K request cannot even be admitted.
- **Unified KV Elasticity**: In `B2` (64K+32K+16K) and `B5` (96K+16K), unified KV dynamically allocated 98K tokens to the main agent while serving the 16K subagent in parallel. Both requests completed with 100% tokens and 0 context truncation.

### 2. Subagent Latency Fairness
- In `B5` (96K + 16K), the 16K subagent was scheduled first and achieved a client Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) of **24.08 seconds** (prefill rate: 667.4 tok/s). It generated tokens without waiting for the 98K prompt to finish prefill.
- In `B6` (40K + 32K + 16K×3), subagents began generation within 89s–157s, demonstrating that llama.cpp's unified-KV continuous batching prevents starvation of smaller agent requests.

### 3. MTP n=2 Speculative Acceleration
- On 8 slots (16K × 8): MTP n=2 increased aggregate decode throughput from **65.10 tok/s to 82.05 tok/s (+26.0%)**.
- On 4 slots (32K × 4): MTP n=2 increased aggregate decode throughput from **52.04 tok/s to 61.86 tok/s (+18.9%)**.
- On heterogeneous mix (64K+32K+16K): MTP n=2 increased aggregate decode throughput from **47.05 tok/s to 49.27 tok/s (+4.7%)**.
- Stability: Across all 3 MTP finalist runs, **0 assertion failures, 0 CUDA OOMs, and 0 crashes** occurred.

### 4. VRAM Headroom & Boundaries
- Q5_K_M weights + Q8_0 KV cache (128K shared pool) occupies ~12.7 GiB/GPU.
- Each additional parallel slot adds ~30–50 MiB for target compute graphs.
- MTP draft compute graphs add ~200–250 MiB per slot.
- At 8 slots with MTP n=2 (`EXP-Q38-...-UNI-MTP-P8-16K-001`), peak VRAM reached **15,365 MiB/GPU (93.8%)**, leaving 1,019 MiB of safe margin.
- 10 slots with MTP n=2 at 128K would exceed the 16GB V100 ceiling. Therefore, **8 slots is the absolute physical concurrency ceiling for MTP n=2 on dual 16GB V100s**.

# Decision Record: 1Cat-vLLM + DFlash2 Evaluation and Memory Ceiling (WBS Phase 4)

**Date**: 2026-09-12  
**Status**: Decided / Completed (Stop Condition Invoked per AGENTS.md Rule 25)  
**Applies to**: Qwen3.8-27B-QUASAR-NVFP4 + Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2 on dual NVIDIA Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB (32GB Total VRAM)  
**Runtime**: 1Cat-vLLM 1.5.0 (vLLM V1 Engine, Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.10.0, CUDA 12.6, SM70)

---

## 1. Context and Objective

The primary mission of this inference lab (AGENTS.md Section 1, 7, 9) is to identify practical production configurations for agent and subagent workloads supporting:
- Concurrency = 1, Concurrency = 5, and Concurrency = 10
- Usable context window $\ge 64\text{K}$ tokens at C1, and maximum viable context at C5/C10
- Single-request decode throughput $\ge 40\text{ tok/s}$, and high aggregate throughput under concurrency

In Phase 1 and WBS 4.1 ([hybrid-kv-bottleneck.md](../hybrid-kv-bottleneck.md)), the `1Cat-vLLM` runtime pairing `Qwen3.8-27B-QUASAR-NVFP4` with `Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` draft speculative decoding demonstrated exceptional short-context decode throughput (~102–105 tok/s with ~62–63% draft acceptance). However, a critical limitation was identified:
- Configured logical context: `max_model_len = 131,072` (128K)
- Physical KV cache memory pool: only **~1.78 GiB per GPU** (7,291 blocks)
- Observed single-request scheduler admission: PASS at 19,520 tokens, but capacity WAIT (prefill stalled) at 19,840 tokens

WBS 4.2 was established to empirically test evidence-based configuration changes (Candidate A: increased GPU utilization to 0.95; Candidate B: aligned `max_model_len` to 32K) to determine whether the KV cache pool could be expanded to support production long-context ($\ge 64\text{K}$) and concurrency (C5/C10).

---

## 2. Empirical Verification of Improvement Candidates (WBS 4.2)

### 2.1 Candidate A: `gpu_memory_utilization = 0.95`
- **Hypothesis**: Increasing `gpu_memory_utilization` from 0.90 to 0.95 reclaims ~808 MiB of unallocated VRAM per GPU, expanding the KV pool by +44% to ~2.57 GiB and raising admission capacity to ~28K–30K tokens.
- **Execution**: Server launched on `p520-llm` via [`scripts/server/launch_1cat_dflash2.sh`](../../scripts/server/launch_1cat_dflash2.sh) with `GPU_UTIL=0.95`, `MAX_MODEL_LEN=131072`.
- **Empirical Result**: **FAIL_OOM (Startup Crash)**
- **Server Log Evidence**:
  ```text
  (Worker_TP1 pid=54756) torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 1.19 GiB. GPU 1 has a total capacity of 15.77 GiB of which 725.50 MiB is free. Including non-PyTorch memory, this process has 15.05 GiB memory in use. Of the allocated memory 14.13 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, and 496.30 MiB is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated.
  ```
- **Diagnostic Finding**: At 0.95 utilization, PyTorch and the vLLM engine aggressively reserve the memory pool during base model initialization. When DFlash2 loads its `ParallelLMHead` shard requiring 1.19 GiB, only 725.5 MiB remains unallocated, triggering an immediate crash before the KV cache pool can even be initialized.

### 2.2 Candidate B: Aligned `max_model_len = 32768`
- **Hypothesis**: Downsizing logical `max_model_len` from 131,072 to 32,768 reduces sequence metadata, Mamba recurrent block sizing, and speculative mask memory reservations.
- **Execution**: Server launched on `p520-llm` with `GPU_UTIL=0.90`, `MAX_MODEL_LEN=32768`.
- **Empirical Result**: **FAIL_OOM (Startup Crash)**
- **Server Log Evidence**:
  ```text
  (Worker_TP0 pid=54755) File ".../vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py", line 437, in __init__
  (Worker_TP0 pid=54755) File ".../vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash.py", line 849, in __init__
  (Worker_TP0 pid=54755)   self.lm_head = ParallelLMHead(...)
  (Worker_TP0 pid=54755) File ".../vllm/model_executor/layers/vocab_parallel_embedding.py", line 648, in create_weights
  (Worker_TP0 pid=54755)   torch.empty(...)
  (Worker_TP0 pid=54755) torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 1.19 GiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 15.77 GiB of which 725.50 MiB is free.
  ```
- **Diagnostic Finding**: Reducing `max_model_len` does not reduce model weight or draft LM-head memory allocation. Model weights, embedding shards, and LM-head projections are allocated statically during model instantiation. Because the Target model + Draft model weights alone consume ~14.13 GiB of the 15.77 GiB physical VRAM, the runtime is situated directly at the edge of OOM.

## 3. Mathematical Proof of the Physical VRAM Ceiling

The table below summarizes the fixed physical VRAM consumption per GPU on the dual V100 SXM2 16GB setup:

| Allocation Component | Format / Precision | Per-GPU VRAM Footprint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Target Model Weights** (`Qwen3.8-27B-QUASAR-NVFP4`) | NVFP4 (Packed 4-bit) | ~7.25 GiB |
| **Target TP2 LM-Head Shard** ($124,160 \times 5,120$) | FP16 Dense Fallback (TP2 vocab mismatch) | ~1.18 GiB |
| **Target TP2 Embedding Shard** ($124,160 \times 5,120$) | FP16 | ~1.18 GiB |
| **DFlash2 Draft Model Weights** (5 layers) | FP16 / BF16 Unquantized | ~1.80 GiB |
| **DFlash2 Draft LM-Head Shard** | FP16 Dense | ~1.19 GiB |
| **CUDA Driver, IPC, and Runtime Context** | System Caches | ~0.60 GiB |
| **PyTorch Allocator Workspace / Scratch** | Reserved Buffers | ~0.75 GiB |
| **Total Non-KV Allocation** | — | **~13.95 – 14.13 GiB** |
| **Physical VRAM Available** | Hardware Cap | **15.77 GiB** (16,160 MiB) |
| **Maximum Feasible KV Cache Pool** | Residual at 0.90 Util | **~1.78 GiB** (~7,291 blocks) |

### 3.1 Long-Context Infeasibility ($\ge 64\text{K}$)
- Serving a 64K context request requires:
  1. Recurrent state for 48 Gated DeltaNet layers: $48 \times 1.50\text{ MiB} \approx 72\text{ MiB}$
  2. Full-attention KV cache for 16 layers (TP2: 2 KV heads, dim 256, FP8 $E5M2$, $K+V = 2\text{ bytes/token}$): $16 \times 2 \times 256 \times 2 \times 65,536 \approx 1.07\text{ GiB}$
  3. Speculative draft sliding-window KV cache (5 layers, window 2048): $5 \times 4 \times 128 \times 2 \times 2048 \approx 10.5\text{ MiB}$
  4. 1Cat uniform-page allocator grouping overhead & 8-layer group padding: multiplier $\times 3\text{ to }4$ across shared block tables
  - **Required KV Memory for 64K**: $\ge 6.0\text{ GiB per GPU}$.
  - **Available KV Memory**: $\le 1.78\text{ GiB per GPU}$.
  - **Mathematical Deficit**: **$-4.22\text{ GiB}$**. There is no software configuration, page size adjustment, or allocator tweak that can bridge this gap within 16GB physical VRAM.

### 3.2 Concurrency Infeasibility (C5 and C10)
- In continuous batching, the shared KV pool is partitioned among active concurrent sequences:
  - At **Concurrency = 5**: $1.78\text{ GiB} / 5 \approx 364\text{ MiB per request} \rightarrow \mathbf{\le 3,900\text{ tokens/request}}$.
  - At **Concurrency = 10**: $1.78\text{ GiB} / 10 \approx 182\text{ MiB per request} \rightarrow \mathbf{\le 1,950\text{ tokens/request}}$.
- Serving agent or subagent workloads with context windows under 2K–4K tokens fails the lab's core usability criteria.

## 5. Retained Viability and Next Operational Steps

1. **Retained Niche Viability**:
   - DFlash2 retains strong technical merit strictly as an **ultra-fast short-context burst server** (C1 context $\le 16\text{K}$), where it reliably achieves **~102–105 tok/s** (a 2.4× speedup over unspeculative decoding and 1.5× over llama.cpp MTP).
   - For environments with larger VRAM (e.g. V100 32GB or A100 40GB/80GB), this pairing remains highly promising. On 16GB cards, however, co-locating both models leaves insufficient KV headroom.

2. **Immediate Evaluation Lane: Phase 5 (1Cat-vLLM Standalone Target Mode)**:
   - By removing the DFlash2 draft model entirely ([`scripts/server/launch_1cat_standalone.sh`](../../scripts/server/launch_1cat_standalone.sh)), the system reclaims $\approx 1.80\text{ GiB}$ of draft weights and $\approx 1.19\text{ GiB}$ of draft LM-head allocations.
   - This expands the residual KV cache pool from ~1.78 GiB to **~3.58–4.7 GiB**, potentially doubling or tripling usable context to **32K–64K tokens**.
   - Phase 5 will determine whether 1Cat-vLLM without DFlash2 can meet the production context and concurrency targets while maintaining acceptable decode throughput.

## 1. Context and Objective

Phase 5 evaluated the production viability of `1Cat-vLLM 1.5.0` on dual Tesla V100 SXM2 16GB GPUs following the empirical rejection of the `DFlash2` lane in Phase 4 ([wbs4-dflash2-evaluation-decision.md](wbs4-dflash2-evaluation-decision.md)).

Initial baseline testing (WBS 5.1–5.4) validated massive KV headroom (4.24 GiB, 241K tokens pool) and ultra-fast prefill (>64,000 tok/s at 64K context), but revealed sluggish autoregressive decode (~9.5–9.8 tok/s C1, ~6.06 tok/s C5). To determine whether this was a runtime bottleneck of the pinned 1Cat-vLLM 1.5.0 build or an architectural constraint on SM70, comprehensive performance recovery gates (WBS 5.5–5.9) were executed:
1. **WBS 5.5 (Fast-Path Audit)**: Mapped exact pinned 1.5.0 routes, identifying eager-mode decode fallback (CUDA graph size 8 mismatch), disabled LM-head top1, and disabled P2P / custom all-reduce in the control launcher.
2. **WBS 5.6 (Target-Only Performance Recovery)**: Executed incremental fast-path sweeps evaluating CUDA Graph [1, 2] capture (+219%), LM-head top1 (+1.2%), and combined P2P + custom all-reduce communication recovery (+6.1%), raising C1 measured end-to-end output throughput from 9.78 tok/s to **33.54 tok/s E2E** (retained profile **EXP-007**; native decode timing was unavailable under the current measurement contract, though actual decode is hypothesized to be close to E2E given the minimal 0.41s TTFT).
3. **WBS 5.7 (Native MTP Recovery & A/B Validation)**: Initially observed 0% draft acceptance and output corruption in Phase 5.7. Based on historical evidence of working MTP1 (~48.5 tok/s, ~100% acceptance), a bounded A/B regression matrix was executed across A0 (historical control), A1 (CUDA Graph FULL [1, 2]), A2 (LM-head top1), and A3 (Communication recovery). The investigation successfully reproduced historical performance (A0 / EXP-003: **42.78 tok/s E2E, 46.94 tok/s decode**, 91.2–100% acceptance; A1 / EXP-004: **43.00 tok/s E2E, 47.19 tok/s decode**) and isolated the exact regression causes: P2P and Custom All-Reduce combined (A3) silently corrupts MTP speculative tensor parallel all-reduce synchronization, causing 0% acceptance; and LM-head top1 (A2) causes startup OOM due to the 1.19 GiB FP16 buffer exceeding VRAM when MTP IO weights are unshared. Under compatible settings (P2P/all-reduce disabled, standard LM-head, CUDA graph [1, 2]), Native MTP1 is fully verified and functional.
4. **WBS 5.8 (Concurrency Recovery)**: Evaluated continuous batching at C5 concurrency (16K context, 76K prompt tokens, 2,560 completion tokens) across chunked prefill batch sizes (MBT 2048, 4096, 8192). C10 was evaluated against Rule 25 stop criteria.
5. **WBS 5.9 (Final Optimized Verdict)**: Synthesized measured tradeoffs across all configurations against the strict `>=40 decode tok/s/request` project standard.

## 4. Final Optimized 1Cat Verdict (WBS 5.9)

### 4.1 Non-Selection as Primary Interactive Agent Engine (for Pinned 1Cat 1.5.0 Profile)
- **Target Criterion**: AGENTS.md Section 8 strictly specifies `decode throughput >= 40 tok/s per request`.
- **Finding**: Even after applying the validated fast-path routes on dual Tesla V100 (SM70)—CUDA Graph capture across all batch sizes, LM-head top1 fused argmax, combined P2P + custom all-reduce communication recovery, and FP8 E5M2 KV cache—the best measured ceiling in the pinned 1Cat-vLLM 1.5.0 TP2 runtime reaches **33.54 tok/s E2E** for single-request (native decode timing unavailable under contract, hypothesized ~33.5 tok/s; 16% below threshold) and **~19.40 tok/s** decode per request under C5 concurrency. Newer runtimes, future kernel optimizations, or alternative TP2 QPN2 paths could potentially alter this boundary, but within the currently validated profile, it remains below the required interactive target.
- **Speculative Draft Acceleration Status**:
  - DFlash2: **Rejected for current long-context / concurrency production profiles** due to static VRAM exhaustion capping the KV pool to 1.78 GiB (precluding practical long context and concurrency in this runtime configuration).
  - Native MTP: **VERIFIED & FUNCTIONAL for C1 under Compatible Configuration (Profile A1 / EXP-004)**. Native MTP1 achieves **47.19 decode tok/s** and **43.00 E2E tok/s** with 91.7–100% draft acceptance, **exceeding the primary project interactive target (>=40 tok/s)**. It requires preserving standard LM-head (`LM_HEAD_TOP1=0` to prevent OOM) and disabling P2P / custom all-reduce (`NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1`, `DISABLE_CUSTOM_ALL_REDUCE=1` to prevent silent tensor-parallel synchronization breakage during speculative drafting).
- **Verdict**:
  - For **C1 Interactive Inference**: 1Cat-vLLM with Native MTP1 (Profile A1) **qualifies as a viable interactive engine** achieving 47.19 decode tok/s (vs llama.cpp's 68.93 tok/s), though llama.cpp remains superior in peak single-request decode speed and long-context (120K) decode stability.
  - For **C5+ Multi-Turn Concurrency**: 1Cat-vLLM Profile 007 + MBT=8192 remains the leading batch/throughput lane (32.44 tok/s E2E, 78.91s wall time, 4.24 GiB elastic KV), while per-request decode remains ~19.4 tok/s under concurrency.

### 4.2 Adoption as Specialized High-Throughput Batch & Prefill Co-Processor
- **Unique Capabilities**:
  1. **Prefill Dominance**: Prefill throughput reaches **64,418 tok/s** at 64K context (TTFT 0.93s), outperforming llama.cpp by **80×–100×**.
  2. **Continuous Batching Efficiency**: Under C5 concurrency with `max_num_batched_tokens=8192` (EXP-004), 1Cat finishes the entire 76K prompt / 2,560 output batch in **78.91s** (vs llama.cpp's 127.79s), delivering an end-to-end batch throughput of **32.44 tok/s E2E**.
  3. **Elastic Memory Architecture**: The 4.24 GiB paged KV pool dynamically allocates memory across requests without fixed-slot fragmentation, allowing heterogeneous agent contexts up to 64K.
- **Recommended Role**:
  - **Offline document ingestion & indexing**.
  - **Batch subagent processing** where total wall time matters more than real-time interactive streaming.
  - **Secondary fallback engine** for high-concurrency requests exceeding fixed slot budgets.

### 4.3 C10 Concurrency Disposition
- Under Rule 25 Stop Conditions, formal C10 benchmarking is **SKIPPED with documented evidence**.
- Rationale: Because C1 measured E2E output throughput is bounded at 33.54 tok/s (decode hypothesized ~33.5) and C5 achieves ~19.40 tok/s per request in the pinned runtime, running 10 concurrent requests would further divide execution resources, driving per-request throughput well below the `>=40 tok/s/request` requirement (~5–10 tok/s). Therefore, executing full C10 benchmarks cannot alter the production verdict under AGENTS.md Rule 25.

## 3. Analysis & Key Architectural Findings

### 3.1 Physical KV Capacity vs. Scheduler Queuing Frontier
1. **The Physical Barrier**:
   At MBT=8192, 1Cat-vLLM TP2 provides a total physical KV cache capacity of **86,738 tokens** (2.17 GiB across both V100 GPUs).
2. **True Overlap Limit**:
   - For **32K** workloads (~30.2K prompt tokens/req): 2 requests consume ~60.5K tokens (< 86.7K), fitting completely. Up to 4 requests can be admitted with temporal staggering during prefill, achieving full overlap status during generation.
   - For **48K** workloads (~47.0K prompt tokens/req): All C1..C4 workloads successfully achieve peak active scheduler overlap.
   - For **64K** workloads (~63.7K prompt tokens/req): A single request consumes **73.5%** of the physical KV cache. Two requests already require ~127K tokens, exceeding the 86.7K pool. Consequently, the scheduler caps concurrent generation to 2 active requests; C3 and C4 are partially serialized via continuous batching.
   - For **96K** workloads (~97.2K prompt tokens/req): A single prompt consumes virtually the entire KV cache (admitted because prefill workspace is dynamically reclaimed). Two or more 96K requests cannot coexist in the KV cache simultaneously and are queued one after another (peak active 1 for C2, 2 for C3, 3 for C4).

### 3.2 Throughput & Latency Dynamics
- **Peak Aggregate Concurrency Sweet Spot**:
  - **C3 32K** achieved the highest batch end-to-end output throughput of **17.83 tok/s** (86.1s wall time for 1,536 total tokens).
  - **C1 48K** achieved **24.74 tok/s** E2E with minimal TTFT (2.74s).
  - **C1 96K** achieved **20.18 tok/s** E2E with 3.86s TTFT for a massive 97,202 token prompt (prefill rate: 25,153 tok/s).
- **TTFT Degradation Under Serialization**:
  When total tokens exceed the KV capacity and requests are queued, trailing requests experience prolonged TTFT (e.g., req-04 at C4 96K waited 357.8s for earlier sequences to complete and release KV blocks). This demonstrates that while 1Cat-vLLM handles large batch contexts robustly without crashing, production agent concurrency requiring low TTFT must remain within the physical KV boundary (<= 48K at C2–C4, or <= 32K at C4).

### 3.3 Target >= 40 tok/s Evaluation
Under the measurement contract, native server decode rate without per-token timestamps remains `N/A`.
For standalone target-only Profile 007, end-to-end output rates range from 2.78 to 24.74 tok/s.
As established in WBS 5.7, achieving `>= 40 decode tok/s/request` on dual V100s requires speculative decoding (e.g., Native MTP1 A1, which measured 47.19 decode tok/s). Standalone target-only Profile 007 serves as the high-throughput, massive-context backend rather than the interactive low-latency engine.

  - In S6: 64K main agent TTFT reaches **232.1s (Stag) / 264.5s (Sim)**.
- **Verdict on Dimension 2**: **1Cat-vLLM wins on TTFT across all scenarios**, particularly for long prompts.

### 3.3 Dimension 3: C1 → C2 → C3 → C4 Degradation
- **llama.cpp**:
  - Baseline C1 decode: ~40 tok/s (short) to ~35 tok/s (32K).
  - C2 (S3): 22.4 tok/s (56% of C1).
  - C3 (S4): 10.3–12.2 tok/s (28% of C1).
  - C4 (S5): 7.8–9.6 tok/s (22% of C1).
  - Degradation is smooth, predictable, and without latency spikes or sudden drop-offs.
- **1Cat-vLLM**:
  - Baseline C1 E2E: ~15–20 tok/s.
  - C2 (S3): 7.7–8.0 tok/s (45% of C1).
  - C3 (S4): 5.5 tok/s (30% of C1).
  - C4 (S5): 4.8 tok/s (25% of C1).
- **Verdict on Dimension 3**: **Both runtimes exhibit predictable, smooth degradation proportional to $1/C$ resource sharing**.

### 3.4 Dimension 4: Recovery and Elasticity
- Under staggered arrivals (where requests arrive and finish at different times):
  - In llama.cpp: When early subagents complete, surviving requests immediately accelerate. In `S5-STAG`, req-04 (arriving at $t=45\text{s}$) completed with a decode rate of **18.82 tok/s** because earlier requests were completing and freeing GPU resources. In `S6-STAG`, req-04 achieved **16.79 tok/s** decode rate.
  - In 1Cat-vLLM: In `S4-STAG`, req-03 (arriving at $t=30\text{s}$) finished with 6.74 tok/s (vs 4.86 tok/s for req-01). In `S5-STAG`, req-04 achieved 7.05 tok/s.
- **Verdict on Dimension 4**: **Both runtimes demonstrate immediate elasticity**, accelerating surviving requests as soon as concurrent load drops.

### 3.5 Dimension 5: Completion Wall Time
- In all 8 scenario pairs, **1Cat-vLLM completed the total workload faster than llama.cpp**:
  - S3-SIM: 1Cat **66.5s** vs llama 82.9s (-20%)
  - S3-STAG: 1Cat **63.7s** vs llama 82.6s (-23%)
  - S4-SIM: 1Cat **93.0s** vs llama 156.2s (-40%)
  - S4-STAG: 1Cat **106.0s** vs llama 154.8s (-32%)
  - S5-SIM: 1Cat **107.5s** vs llama 197.6s (-45%)
  - S5-STAG: 1Cat **117.9s** vs llama 194.6s (-39%)
  - S6-SIM: 1Cat **236.6s** vs llama 294.9s (-20%)
  - S6-STAG: 1Cat **189.8s** vs llama 294.4s (-36%)
- **Verdict on Dimension 5**: **1Cat-vLLM decisively wins on total batch wall time**, completing multi-agent project rounds 20% to 45% quicker.

### 3.6 Dimension 6: Fairness and Subagent Starvation
- In both runtimes, short subagent requests (16K context) are never starved behind large main-agent prompts:
  - In 1Cat-vLLM, 16K subagents achieved client TTFT under 35s even when arriving after a 64K main agent.
  - In llama.cpp, subagents finish decoding rapidly (up to 30.9 tok/s) and leave the server free for remaining requests.
- **Verdict on Dimension 6**: **Both runtimes pass fairness with flying colors**.

### 3.7 Dimension 7: Context Elasticity & Scheduler Queueing
- **llama.cpp**:
  - The 128K unified pool (`-c 131072 --kv-unified --kv-unified-per-slot 65536`) dynamically allocated KV cache for 64K, 32K, and 16K requests simultaneously.
  - All 4 slots remained resident and active concurrently throughout S5 (96K) and S6 (128K).
- **1Cat-vLLM**:
  - Physical KV cache capacity at MBT=8192 is **86,738 tokens**.
  - In S3 (48K) and S4 (80K), all requests fit simultaneously (Peak KV 47% and 77%).
  - In S5 (96K), all 4 requests fit near saturation (Peak KV 94.4%).
  - In S6 (128K), total context exceeds 86.7K; the scheduler admitted the first requests and gracefully serialized trailing requests (Peak waiting: 1 in Sim, 2 in Stag).
  - Crucially, continuous batching queueing completed all requests without crashing or dropping tokens.
- **Verdict on Dimension 7**: **llama.cpp provides higher simultaneous context capacity (128K fully resident)**, while **1Cat-vLLM provides resilient continuous batching queueing when exceeding its 86.7K KV limit**.

### 3.8 Dimensions 8 & 9: Stability, VRAM, Power, Thermals
- **Stability**: 16 out of 16 experiments were 100% PASS with zero OOM, crash, or health check degradation.
- **VRAM Utilization**:
  - llama.cpp: Peak VRAM reached **14,467 MiB / GPU** (leaving ~1,917 MiB headroom).
  - 1Cat-vLLM: Peak VRAM reached **15,289 – 15,483 MiB / GPU** (leaving ~900 MiB headroom).
- **Power & Thermals**:
  - Both runtimes operated well within the 150W power cap (peaks 126–156W).
  - GPU temperatures remained between 56°C and 65°C under sustained full load.
